newsitem.title: USA: Spain, Portugal could meet '99 EMU target - ABN.
newsitem.headline: Spain, Portugal could meet '99 EMU target - ABN.

text.p: European Monetary Union will likely be introduced on schedule in January of 1999 and include Spain, Portugal and Sweden but not Britain, a senior European bank executive said on Friday.

After this week's International Monetary Fund/World Bank meeting, it appears likely that 12 countries will be in the core group that will initially make up the union, Dolf van den Brink, senior executive vice president of the Netherlands' ABN AMRO Bank, said in a speech here.
"Before this IMF conference this week, I was convinced that only Ireland and Finland were to join this first group as well," said van den Brink, who attended the conference.
"But from conversations during the IMF conference this week, I've learned that also Sweden, Portugal and Spain are going to do their utmost to join the first group," he said.
If Spain and Portugal succeed, it is unlikely Italy would remain behind, he added.
"It is unimaginable to me that Italy stays out when Spain and Portugal join the first group," he said.
"This will place also the U.K. in a very difficult position. They are condemned to be in a group together with Denmark and Greece," he said.
That would make the core group of 12 consist of Germany, France, Belgium, Austria, Holland, Luxembourg, Ireland, Finland, Sweden, Italy, Spain and Portugal, he said.

Most of these countries will not have trouble meeting inflation and interest rate targets, he said. And while some may have difficulty meeting budget deficit targets of three percent of GDP by 1997, as set out in the Maastricht Treaty, he believes Spain, Portugal and Italy will "do more than originally expected."
In terms of the effect on the U.S. markets, van den Brink said turmoil in Europe leading up to 1999, when the core group will fix its exchange rates, could support the dollar.

"But after that, when EMU is firmly established, the U.S. currency will see some serious competition out of Europe," he said, adding that the euro could eventually replace the U.S. dollar as the world's reserve currency.
However, former U.S. Treasury Secretary Lloyd Bentsen, who also spoke at the conference, was skeptical.

"I think it's important Europe be strong, I think it's important Europe be profitable, I wish them well in their endeavor," he said. "When they talk about replacing the United States dollar as reserve currency, I don't believe it."
He did not elaborate further, other than to say the euro could be a competitive force in the long run.
